analysis.investment_thesis: Pearl Global is a genuinely improving business — EBIT CAGR of 23.8% and ROIC ~22% — but the Magic Formula rejects it on price: earnings yield of ~5.3% (EBIT 417 Cr / EV ~7,844 Cr) sits well below the 6% minimum, meaning you're overpaying for a thin-margin apparel manufacturer. Wait for a cheaper entry or margin expansion that justifies the multiple.
key_strengths: ROIC/ROCE ~22%, clearing the Magic Formula's 20% threshold — sustained over multiple years
EBIT CAGR 23.8% (9Y) with clear operating leverage: revenue +13.9% vs EBIT +23.8%
China+1 beneficiary with real revenue acceleration — revenue nearly tripled from 2021 (1,491 Cr) to 2025 (4,506 Cr)
key_risks: Earnings yield ~5.3% — stock is expensive on Magic Formula; EV/EBITDA of 18.4x is rich for a 6.3% operating margin business
FCF collapsed to 81 Cr in 2025 vs 229 Cr in 2024 despite higher net profit — capex (119 Cr) and working capital eating cash
Finance costs compounding at 20.4% CAGR; debt grew to 773 Cr, and rising interest burden threatens earnings quality
red_flags: Earnings yield ~5.3% — below the 6% Magic Formula floor, meaning it fails the 'cheap' test entirely
Free cash flow conversion deteriorating sharply: FCF/Net Profit ratio dropped to ~35% in 2025 vs ~136% in 2023
Operating margin of 6.29% leaves almost no buffer — any demand shock, currency move, or cotton price spike destroys earnings
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Running the Magic Formula on Pearl Global: EBIT FY2025 = 417 Cr, Enterprise Value = 7,581 Cr (market cap) + 773 Cr (debt) − 510 Cr (cash) = ~7,844 Cr, yielding an earnings yield of 5.3%. That's a disqualifying number — Greenblatt's formula requires >12% to be interesting, >6% at minimum. On the other side, ROIC proxied by ROCE at 22.1% is legitimate and shows a business that earns decent returns on the capital it deploys. The problem is classic: one leg of the formula works, the other doesn't. The market has already priced in the growth story at P/E 29x and EV/EBITDA 18.4x.

The business trajectory is genuinely impressive — EBIT nearly 7x'd from 61 Cr (2016) to 417 Cr (2025), and it's a real China+1 export play. But the FCF story in 2025 is concerning: despite 231 Cr net profit, free cash flow was only 81 Cr. Capex ran at 119 Cr and operating CF slipped to 176 Cr, suggesting the growth is being funded by working capital stretch and debt (financing CF turned positive at +101 Cr in 2025). Finance costs at 112 Cr are now nearly 27% of EBIT — that's a meaningful drag. Until the stock derate to an earnings yield above 10% or margins structurally improve above 8-9% operating, Pearl Global is a watchlist name, not a buy.
